title: Ordinary words that mean "to restrain"
core: Every word here holds something back without destroying it — the force is still there, still moving, just slowed, capped, steered, or weighed down. That shared meaning is easy; the distinctions live elsewhere. Ask who is applying the restraint (an agent choosing to, or circumstance imposing it), whether it's wanted or resented, and whether the thing restrained is a moving body, a rising quantity, a hot impulse, or an effort in progress. Most of these also hide their GRE sense behind a common everyday one.

words.nuance: **Check** is the arrest of forward motion at a moment — an advance checked at the river, anger checked before it lands. Alone in this group it works as a countable noun for the restraining thing itself (*a check on executive power*), which is why it dominates constitutional and political prose.

**Curb** applies to a quantity or rate you want lower but not zero — inflation, emissions, spending, drinking. It's a dial being turned down over time rather than a body being stopped, and it's the house verb of policy writing: an authority acting deliberately on something with its own upward momentum.

**Bridle** implies steering something powerful you own or command — your tongue, his ambition — so it moralizes in a way the others don't, carrying self-discipline and formal register. It's also the only word here with a second intransitive life: *bridle at* an insult, offence taken for one's dignity and visible in the body.

**Temper** doesn't push against the thing — it adds the opposite ingredient until the result sits in proportion (justice with mercy, zeal with caution). Uniquely in this group the outcome is an improvement, not a diminishment, and the objects are always something running hot.

**Hamper** is the only one where nobody chose the restraint: circumstance imposes it, it's unwanted, and it drags rather than caps. Watch the passive collocation — efforts are *hampered by* rain, budget cuts, missing data — and note the object is an activity in progress, not an impulse or a quantity.

**Inhibit** locates the brake inside the system — a psychological block or a chemical/biological damping, not a hand applied from outside. Cold inhibits growth; the inhibited speaker isn't forbidden, they simply can't get it out, which is why *inhibitions* means shyness rather than rules.

exam_note: Two traps at once: the everyday noun senses (a tick mark, a pavement edge, a picnic basket, losing your temper) are decoys, and once you're in the right sense the answer hinges on whether the restraint is deliberate and desired (check/curb/bridle), improving by admixture (temper), or an unwelcome drag (hamper/inhibit).
